newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-JUVE'S 24TH TITLE VICTORY IS SIGN OF ETERNAL YOUTH.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JUVE'S 24TH TITLE VICTORY IS SIGN OF ETERNAL YOUTH.

text.p: Juventus, the Old Lady of Italian soccer, celebrates her 100th birthday this year but her appetite for success makes her look younger than ever.
Juve's 24th league title, clinched on Friday with a 1-1 draw at Atalanta of Bergamo, was the seventh major trophy in three years for the club known in Italy as "La Vecchia Signora".
Since 1994, the Turin club has won two league titles, a European Cup, the Intercontinental and European Supercups, the Italian Supercup and the Italian Cup.
Next Wednesday, the roll of honour could lengthen if Juventus successfully retain the European Cup by defeating Borussia Dortmund in Munich.

Italian papers left no doubts as to the secret behind Juve's run of success on Saturday. "The incredible years of Lippi", read a headline in the Turin sports daily Tuttosport, referring to coach Marcello Lippi.
Milan's La Gazzetta dello Sport even published a full-page photo of the Juventus manager, under the headline "The Lippi Show".

In a season in which front-line players such as midfielder Antonio Conte, Croat striker Alen Boksic and Italy's Alessandro Del Piero have been blighted by injury, Lippi has marshalled his reserves like a veteran army general.
"Anyone can manage 13 or 14 men but not 20. Lippi can," said an editorial in La Repubblica. "Every time a player fell, even a well-known name, a substitute was ready to take his place."

Again and again this season, maestro Lippi has seamlessly fitted new players into his side and kept on winning. Mark Iuliano, a second division player last season, came in for Moreno Torricelli, veteran Michele Padovano for Boksic and inexperienced striker Christian Vieri for Del Piero.
Lippi's flexibility stretches beyond players to tactics.

When Conte ruptured knee ligaments last autumn, Lippi rapidly abandoned his three-man strikeline in favour of a more conservative four-man midfield with France's Zinedine Zidane in the role of playmaker.

"This was the championship of scientific rotation," concluded Turin daily La Stampa. "It has killed the concept of the ideal formation and destroyed the barriers between first-choice players and substitutes."
Fittingly, circumstances conspired on Friday to leave many of Juventus's first-team players wearing the names of their substitutes on their backs.
In the confusion that followed a pitch invasion three minutes before time, players thought the game was over and swapped shirts with their team mates on the bench.
But after police had cleared the pitch the referee summoned the players back on to the field and Juve's goalscorer Iuliano was seen wearing Torricelli's shirt.
In part, Lippi's ability to switch first- and second-choice players without blunting Juve's winning edge has been forced upon him.

Officially, the club now puts the balance sheet before player loyalty and in the past two seasons the policy has deprived Lippi of top players such as Roberto Baggio, Gianluca Vialli and Fabrizio Ravanelli.
But a winning squad rather than team is part of the Lippi philosophy.
"Juve is a team for which the term solidarity would not be out of place," wrote La Repubblica. "No-one plays the diva."
"This triumph is the fruit of great men rather than champions," said Lippi on Friday.
In their post-season analysis on Saturday, critics singled out midfield grafter Didier Deschamps, a French international, and the entire defence for praise.
"The victory of Juve is also a victory for defence, for (goalkeeper Angelo) Peruzzi and (defenders Ciro) Ferrara and (Uruguayan Paolo) Montero," wrote one pundit.
These same players have formed the backbone of Juve's triumphant march through the Champions' League.
"Now Europe is our main objective," said the club's honorary president Umberto Agnelli. "The double would be the ultimate."
